lines.note: Tocurubuxi is the outer ankle bone; the Portuguese explicitly contrasts the outside with the inner ankle in the following subentry. The initial T has a weak impression but remains legible.
Vchicurubuxi names the inner ankle bone; its gloss continues on the next row. The damaged middle letters agree with the anatomical contrast, without changing the printed initial V.
Dentro completes the definition of Vchicurubuxi as the ankle bone on the inside, rather than beginning another entry.
Tocusa is the rough scouring plant, tokusa; the abraded initial is T, not the OCR F. The Portuguese describes a harsh, abrasive herb and continues with its use.

runs.text: que alimpão, & fazem liſo o pao, ou corno.

lines.note: The plant is used to clean and smooth wood or horn. This practical gloss supports tokusa while retaining the historical spellings alimpão and pao.
Tocuson combines gain and loss, directly glossed as profit and loss; the long s is retained in the headword.
Tocutai is explained by cauaru gui, changing or being replaced; the Portuguese begins an example involving an official or agent. The physical split mudar-/ſe is retained.

runs.text: ſe como algum official, ou feitor, &c.

lines.note: Completes the example of replacing an official or steward. The final S. is a roman usage label for written language, distinct from the italic Portuguese definition.
Tokutoku is an adverb meaning quickly. The example repeats Tocuto-/cu, with t rather than OCR r in the divided reduplication; the abbreviation Adu. and Vt are italic.
Completes tokutoku itoma wo kudasareyo to mooshita: he asked to be granted leave quickly. The Portuguese Diße introduces the translation continuing below.

runs.text: que lhe deße de preßa licença.

lines.note: Completes the request that permission or leave be given promptly. There is a narrow word division between preßa and licença; the historical preßa spelling is not modernized.
Tokusei is a general remission of debts and rents. The Portuguese legal explanation continues across the physical ar-/rendamentos break, with its printed accent retained.

runs.text: rendamentos, que fazem os ſenhores conforme

lines.note: Completes arrendamentos and identifies the lords as granting this remission. Conforme leads into the statement about Japanese custom on the next row.
The debt-remission practice is said to follow the custom of Japan. Iapão is Portuguese within the gloss, not an embedded Japanese term for typeface marking.
Tokushin, paraphrased by kokorouru, means understanding or apprehending. Perce-/ber is a normal physical division of the second Portuguese infinitive.
Completes perceber and gives tokushin itasu, to understand. The short example is part of the same entry and its introductory Vt is italic.
This second Tocuxin is equated with Tocuson and defined as profit and loss. It is a separate entry from the preceding word for understanding; Latin l introduces the variant.

runs.text: Candieiro de pee de ferro, ou outro

lines.note: Toodai is a standing lamp or candle holder made from iron or another metal. The circumflex distinguishes this headword from the caroned Tǒdai below.
After completing the metal specification, kaketoodai names the hanging form of the lamp. Candieiro has a faint internal e, matching the more clearly printed word above.
Dependura completes the description of the hanging lamp. The short row remains part of the kaketoodai subentry.
Toodai with a caron, paraphrased as ima no yo, means the present age. The contrast with the preceding lamp headword requires preserving the different printed vowel marks.

runs.text: Circulo do arco de atirar da parte de

lines.note: Todake refers to the outer portion of a shooting bow. The scan reads atirar, correcting the missing i in OCR atrar; do has no secure separate accent.
Fora completes the outer-bow definition; maedake is then contrasted as the part on the inside. Both Japanese forms belong to the same bow comparison.

Todashi is explained by tori-idasu, to take out. Enlargement shows two dotted i sorts after Tor and a final u, giving Toriidaſu rather than OCR Toridaſi; the whole Portuguese phrase Tirar fora is italic. The historical aita principal part remains unchanged.

runs.text: Interrupção, ou o ceßar algũa couſa.

lines.note: Todaye denotes interruption or the cessation of something. The Japanese corresponds to todae; the y records the historical spelling and is not removed.
Todaye suru is the corresponding verbal construction, to be interrupted or cease. The definition makes explicit the relation between the noun and suru.

runs.text: Cotoxi curofunega todaye xita, l, to-

lines.note: Kotoshi kurofune ga todae shita begins the example of the foreign ship failing to come this year. A visible word space separates Cotoxi from curofunega; the alternative verb continues after to-.
Dayeta completes the alternative todayeta. The Portuguese says that the ship was absent this year; the scan reads a nao, not the OCR fusion amnao.

runs.text: Todaye, uru, eta. l, todaye ſuru.

lines.note: The verb todaye, todayuru, todayeta is equated with todaye suru. Inter begins interromper without a printed terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.

runs.text: romper, ou ceßar por algum tempo.

lines.note: Romper completes interromper, and the second gloss specifies cessation for some time. The physical split does not indicate a separate word in the explanation.

runs.text: Grao, ou dignidade de Bonzos princi-

lines.note: This Toodoo denotes a rank or dignity of leading Buddhist clergy. Its damaged initial is T, not F; the two distinct vowel marks are retained from the print.
Completes principaes and compares those dignitaries with heads of temples. Varelas is the Portuguese temple term used by the gloss; it is not a Japanese headword.
Tǒdǒ, paraphrased as ataru michi, denotes arts belonging to a particular professional line. Both carons are visible and distinguish this entry from the preceding clerical rank.

runs.text: certas familias, & ninguem fora dellas as po-

lines.note: These arts belong to particular families, and people outside those families are excluded from publicly teaching them. Po- continues into pode below.
Completes the restriction on public teaching and introduces toodoo no mei-i, a renowned practitioner within such a discipline. The internal hyphen in mei-i is printed within the line and is retained.

runs.text: Medico inſigne de algũa certa medicina, ou

lines.note: The example is translated as a distinguished physician in a particular medicine or healing tradition. The tilde remains over the u in algũa.
Modo de curar completes the medical comparison as a particular method of treatment. This brief continuation closes the professional-discipline entry.

runs.text: Hum certo animal do mar, que tẽ ca-

lines.note: Todo names a sea animal described here by its physical features. The gloss begins cabelo across the line division; no modern zoological identification is imposed on the transcription.
Completes cabelo and adds that the animal has four feet. These are the source gloss's descriptive features, retained without zoological modernization.
Tǒdo is equated with Morocoxi and Taitǒ and glossed as China. The damaged initial and caron are recoverable; OCR rxdo is not a separate Japanese form.
Toodo is equated with shikato and described as being at ease or securely. The Portuguese deſcã continues into ſadamente below, retaining the nasal abbreviation on a.
Completes descansadamente and gives toodo mono wo woku, to place something securely. The historical voqu spelling is retained rather than normalized to modern oku.
The first example means setting something securely. The second begins toodo go-/zare, an invitation to be at ease, divided across the physical lines.
Zare completes gozare. The Portuguese is the imperative Eſtai, be at your ease; the final i corrects OCR Eſtat and agrees with the Japanese invitation.
Todokoori describes being held up or impeded. The stated principal parts and historical ou sequence are preserved while the explanation continues below.

runs.text: ſe couſa que continua, anda, ou corre como a-

lines.note: The obstruction applies to something that ordinarily continues, moves, or runs, such as water. Continua is visible; OCR eontinua misidentified its initial c.

Completes agoa and gives a clock as another example of interrupted motion. Item introduces the additional sense of a business being deferred, continuing in column 2; the scan supplies relogio, Item, and Differirſe.

runs.text: algum negocio por impedimento, ou outra cou-

lines.note: Continues Differirſe from column 1: some business is delayed by an impediment or another circumstance. A short printed hyphen follows cou at the column edge.

runs.text: ſa que ſobre vem, ou impedirſe alguem que eſ-

lines.note: Completes couſa and describes an intervening event, or a person being prevented from proceeding. The scan supports ſa and the joined impedirſe, correcting OCR ſo and impedi ſe.
Completes eſtava and specifies someone about to travel. The historical pera is retained, and this row closes the verb explanation begun in column 1.

The noun todokoori means an impediment or hindrance. The terminal To. starts the repeated form continued below; enlargement shows a round dot like the nearby full stop, so the printed punctuation is retained despite the divided word.

Completes todokoori mo noo mono wo yuu: speaking without an impediment. The mark over nǒ is a downward caron, confirmed by comparison with yǔ on the same line; the unexpected mark is preserved rather than normalized. The Portuguese begins Falar com, with a visible final m and no secure terminal hyphen.
Corrente sem embaraço describes fluent, unimpeded speech, completing the example above. Its printed wording is retained without inserting an omitted noun or regularizing the construction.
Todomari is to stop or cease. The abbreviated principal parts are retained exactly as printed rather than expanded into modern Japanese forms.
Jigai wo todomaru means refraining from killing oneself. Initial Ii functions as consonantal Ji here, as the Portuguese translation makes clear.
Completes the preceding definition as killing oneself. The printed aßi meſmo is retained as the reflexive Portuguese expression, without modern orthographic normalization.
Todome is the transitive counterpart, making something cease or stopping it. This leads into the example of delivering a finishing stroke.
Todome wo sasu means delivering the finishing stroke. The Portuguese specifies cutting the throat, and the final ſò- continues into mente below; OCR fi- misread the damaged word.

runs.text: mente aguela, ou todo o peſcoço.

lines.note: Mente completes ſòmente, followed by cutting the throat or the whole neck. The initial m is abraded but its surviving strokes fit the continuation; the row is indented like the surrounding gloss lines.
Todoke is explained as persevering or continuing with something. This historical verbal use precedes the delivery and notification senses later in the entry.

runs.text: com algũa couſa. Ajuntaſe às raizes dos ver-

lines.note: The grammatical explanation says that this verb joins the roots or stems of other verbs. The ending ver- continues into verbos on the next physical row.

Completes verbos and illustrates persevering in observing a law: go-okite wo tamochi todokuru. The first o of Govoqiteuo has a faint fleck above it, but no secure two-stroke caron; the unmarked reading is adopted with this graphic caveat.
The Portuguese translates continuing to observe this law. A visible separation gives deſta ley; Yacuſo- begins yakusoku in the next example.

Completes yakusoku wo todokuru, fulfilling a promise. The expected o between tod and quru is not securely visible in the abraded gap, so tod quru is retained literally; the intended verb is identifiable from its repeated forms. Comprir retains the printed historical vowel.
Fumi nado wo todokuru describes delivering a letter or similar item. The Portuguese reads fiel-, continued by mente below, not OCR ful-.

runs.text: mente a carta, ou outra couſa. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Completes fielmente and specifies faithful delivery of a letter or another object. Item then opens an additional meaning continued on the next row.

runs.text: Dar conta, ou fazer a ſaber a

lines.note: Todokuru is now explained as reporting or making something known to another. The initial paragraph mark in OCR is not present on this physical row; the preceding row already carries the section marker.
Completes the reporting gloss and gives a regional Ximo usage: dying in war. Ximo is the Japanese place label embedded within Portuguese explanation and is set in roman type.
Completes guerra and specifies death in the service of one's lord. The initial letter of ſeruiço is long s, not f; the sense is service rather than a different noun.
The noun todoke is endurance or perseverance. Co begins the following koguchi example; no terminal hyphen is supplied where none is secure in the scan.
Koguchi de todoke wo shita illustrates the regional military sense; the Portuguese says he died in war. The physical Co/guchide split is retained.
Completes guerra; the final upright X. is the regional usage label for Ximo. Its full stop belongs with the roman label, not the italic gloss.

runs.text: Perſeuerar atè o fim, ou che-

lines.note: Todoki means persevering to the end or reaching a goal. The abraded initial is T rather than OCR F; che- continues into chegar below.
Completes chegar and gives yorozu ni todokanu hito ja, a person who does not carry things through. The negative todocanu supplies the contrast with perseverance.

runs.text: He homem inconſtante, ou que quebra facilmẽ

lines.note: The example describes an inconstant person who readily breaks a promise. The scan shows the nasal abbreviation facilmẽ continuing into te; no unconfirmed terminal hyphen is supplied.
Completes facilmente and the promise-breaking gloss. Ienno michinito- then begins persevering in the path of virtue; initial Ie here carries the consonantal reading zen.
Doqu completes todoqu, and the Portuguese explicitly gives persevering in the path of virtue. The end of virtude has d and e, correcting OCR virtule.
Te ga todoku means that the hand reaches. The Portuguese abranger a introduces reaching or extending the hand to some place on the following line.
The hand reaches some place, completing the preceding example. The printed mão and algũa retain their distinct tilde carriers.
Todorokashi means making a rumbling noise. The example begins kuruma wo to-/dorokasu, causing a cart to rattle; Vt is italic.

runs.text: Fazer eſtrondo cõ o carro q̃ rãge.

lines.note: Completes todorokasu and translates the noise made by a creaking cart. The nasal abbreviations cõ, q̃, and rãge remain unexpanded.
The reduplicated expression first describes a weak or unsteady manner of walking. The terminal co- continues into como; enlargement of the column edge confirms its short, heavy hyphen.
Completes como pera cair, as though about to fall. The example repeats todoro todoroto before ayu-/mu, walking in this manner.
Mu completes ayumu, and the Portuguese restates walking in that manner. Item then begins another sense rather than a new headword.

runs.text: Modo de fazer eſtrondo o carro que vai rangẽ

lines.note: The next sense concerns the rumbling of a cart as it creaks along. The visible tilde in rangẽ represents the omitted nasal before do on the following row; it is not expanded.

runs.text: do, ou com difficuldade por ruins caminhos,

lines.note: Completes rangendo and adds the difficulty of travelling over bad roads. This explains the cart-noise sense of the reduplicated expression.

runs.text: &c. ¶ Item, Modo de ſoarẽ trouões cõ tra-

lines.note: A further sense describes the sound of thunder with a crashing noise. The split tra-/quinada is retained, as are the abbreviating tildes in ſoarẽ and cõ.
Quinada completes traquinada, followed by fury in the thunder description. The next example begins todoro todoro-/to fuminaraſu, stamping or treading with a loud rumble.
Completes the Japanese example, making a stamping noise with the feet. The final Portuguese word is pès, with s rather than OCR r; the printed grave accent is retained.
Walking over boards is given as an example of that loud footfall. This completes the preceding illustration rather than opening the next verb entry.
Todoroki denotes the creaking or sounding of cart wheels. The abraded Japanese consonants are clarified by the related entries and the visible strokes, without altering its u, ita principal parts.

runs.text: rodas do carro que vão paßando pellas pedras.

lines.note: The cart wheels make the sound while passing over stones. The printed historical forms paßando and pellas are retained.

runs.text: Modo de ſoar o taboado, ou algũa

lines.note: Todoroto describes the sound of wooden flooring or a bridge. The Portuguese object continues onto the following row.

Completes the bridge description as one crossed by horses, then begins the Japanese example with Na-. The phrase continues on f0509 with gafaxiuo, making nagahashi; the detached gafaxi below is its catchword, not an additional body row.
